(p-٤٩٩٠)Surat Ya-Sin

It is Meccan. Some scholars excepted from it His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent ahead and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12], and the verse that follows, on the basis of what al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Banu Salama were in the outskirts of Medina. They wanted to move closer to the mosque, so this verse was revealed."

There is no need to claim an exception in this verse or in similar ones, because that claim rests on taking "revelation" (nuzul) to mean that the incident was the cause of the verse's descent. In fact, revelation in the sense of the verse's applicability includes that, and everything the verse applies to, as we have explained many times, especially in the introduction. This is supported by the fact that this narration states that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse to them, as in the report of the two Sahihs. The same applies to what is reported about the verse ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47] from this surah, that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. The intended meaning is what we have mentioned. The authors of the marginal glosses (hawashi) did not arrive at this verification here, so keep it in mind. Its number of verses is eighty-three.

Among what has been reported about its virtue is what al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Anas, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin." Its chain contains weakness.

(p-٤٩٩١)In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Ya-Sin﴾.

﴿Ya-Sin﴾: The discussion of such opening letters has been covered many times before. Its essence, as Abu al-Su'ud stated, is that they are either recited in sequence as a listing, so they have no share in grammatical analysis (i'rab), or they are a name for the surah, as Khalil and Sibawayh explicitly affirmed, and this is the view of most scholars. In that case their position is either nominative, as a deleted predicate, or accusative, as an object of a deleted verb. Both possibilities are the basis of the reading of ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ in the nominative and accusative cases.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[2] ﴿By the wise Qur'an﴾.

﴿By the wise Qur'an﴾: that is, possessing wisdom (al-hikmah), or speaking with wisdom. Since the station of wisdom (al-hikmah) among the forms of knowledge is like the station of the head, and it is the most distinctive of the attributes of the revelation (al-tanzil), it was preferred in the oath by it over the rest of its attributes, for this reason.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[3–4] ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers, on a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin: 4].

﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers, on a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin: 4]. The straight path (ṣirāṭ mustaqīm) is that which leads to the desired goal without fatigue (lughūb). The indefinite form (tankīr) is for magnification and glorification (tafkhīm wa-ta'ẓīm).

[5] ﴿Revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾.

﴿Revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ is in the accusative (naṣb) by supposing a verb for it (ʿalā idmār fiʿlihi), and in the nominative (rafʿ) as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of ﴿Yā, Sīn﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 1] if it is a name of the surah, or if it is treated as referring to it (muʾawwalan bihā). The clause containing the oath is parenthetical (muʿtariḍah), and the oath serves to emphasize both what is sworn to (al-muqsam ʿalayhi) and that by which the oath is sworn (al-muqsam bihi), out of concern for it (ihtimāman).

The discussion of His words, Exalted is He:

[6] ﴿So that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless.﴾

﴿So that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾, meaning: with no messenger and no scripture. ﴿So they are heedless﴾, meaning: of the matter of the truth concerning the Creator and the created, through disbelief, corruption, and denial of the Resurrection and the Return.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Saying, Exalted is He:

[7] ﴿Indeed, the word has come into effect against most of them, so they do not believe.﴾

﴿Indeed, the word has come into effect against most of them﴾: that is, they have become deserving that punishment should descend upon them and that they be avenged with the utmost severity. ﴿So they do not believe﴾: that is, they do not wish to believe and be guided, out of disbelief, arrogance, obstinacy, and transgression upon the earth without right.

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[8] ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, and they reach up to their chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, and they reach up to their chins﴾: that is, to the beards; meaning they extend to them and are fastened to them. ﴿So they are held with their heads raised﴾: that is, raising their heads and lowering their gaze. It is said: "aqmaha al-rajul" (he raised his head and lowered his gaze). And "aqmaha al-ghull al-asir" means that the shackle left the captive's head raised because of its tightness, so he is "muqmah." This happens when the pole of the shackle, which pokes his chin, does not let him lower his head.

Ibn al-Athir said: The phrase in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they reach up to their chins﴾ is a metaphor for the hands, not for the necks, because the shackle brings the hand close to the chin and the neck, and it is near the chin. Al-Azhari said: God, mighty and majestic, meant that when their hands were shackled at their necks, the shackles raised their chins and heads upward, like camels raising their heads. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn Kathir: he mentioned the shackle at the neck and omitted the hands, although both are intended, since the context indicates it; for the shackle is recognized only as that which joins the hands with the neck.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[ 9 ] ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they cannot see.﴾

﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they cannot see.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: He depicted their obstinacy in disbelief, and that there is no way to bring them back from it, by making them like the shackled, head-raised prisoners, in that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks towards it, nor lower their heads to it. And [He made them] like those enclosed between two barriers, unable to see what is before them or behind them, in that they have no reflection or insight, and that they are blind to looking at the signs of God. End of quote. That is, the whole is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*, a metaphor built on an extended image).

In *al-Intisaf* by al-Nasir: If you separate this comparison, their obstinacy in disbelief is likened to the fetters, and their arrogance in refusing to accept the truth, and in submitting and humbling themselves to hear it, is likened to the raised heads (*al-iqmah*), because the one with raised head does not lower it. His saying, ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], is a completion of the constraint of the raised heads upon them. The absence of reflection on the earlier generations is likened to a barrier behind them, and the absence of consideration of future consequences is likened to a barrier before them. End of quote. Thus there is a multiple comparison in it. Al-Shihab said: The allegorical depiction is better than this. End of quote.

Then al-Nasir said: It is possible that the *fa'* in ﴿so they are raising their heads﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8] is for sequence, like the first *fa'*, or for causation. There is no doubt that the pressing of the hand together with the neck in the fetter necessitates the raised head; for the hand, God forbid, remains holding the fetter beneath the chin, pushing it away and preventing it from being trodden upon. The comparison would be more complete on this interpretation, for when the hand is free and unbound, the shackled person has some relief through its release, and perhaps he may devise by it a way of freeing himself from the fetter; but this is not so when it is bound. To what we have mentioned of the separate comparisons, we add that the closing of the doors of stratagem upon them, in guidance and in releasing themselves from the noose of disbelief decreed upon them, is likened to the fetters of the hands, for the hand is the instrument of the stratagem for escape. End of quote.

This was chosen because what comes before it and after it concerns their conditions in this world, whereas Abu Hayyan took it to describe their conditions in the Hereafter, as a literal statement containing no comparison. That view is open to objection, that it would then be an extraneous element in the context; its justification as an explanation of His saying, ﴿the word has become due against most of them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7], is possible, but the first view is more precise and more deserving of acceptance.

﴿And it is alike to them whether you warn them﴾ means: whether you frighten them with the Qur'an. ﴿Or do not warn them, they will not believe﴾ means: they do not want to believe. [18] ﴿They said: "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you."﴾

**Remarks:**

**The first:** Ibn Kathir said: It has been related from many of the early scholars (salaf) that this town was Antioch (Antakiyya), and that these three were messengers from Jesus, peace be upon him, as Qatada and others stated. This is the view that is not reported from any of the later exegetes other than him. There are several objections to this:

First: The apparent meaning of the story indicates that these were messengers of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not from the side of Jesus, peace be upon him, as He says: ﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14]. Had these been among the disciples (hawariyyun), they would have used an expression suited to their being from Jesus, peace be upon him. And Allah knows best. Moreover, if they had been messengers of Jesus, they would not have said to them: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾.

Second: The people of Antioch believed in the messengers of Jesus sent to them, and they were the first city to believe in Jesus. For this reason, among the Christians it was one of the four cities that have patriarchs (batariqa), namely: Jerusalem (al-Quds), because it is the city of Jesus; Antioch, because it was the first city to believe in Jesus after its people; Alexandria (al-Iskandariyya), because in it they agreed on the appointment of patriarchs, bishops (asaqifa), deacons (shammasa), and priests (rahabin); and then Rome (Rumiyya), because it is the city of King Constantine, who supported their religion and strengthened it. When he founded Constantinople (al-Qustantiniyya), they moved the patriarch from Rome to it, as was mentioned by more than one of those who recorded their histories, such as Sa'id ibn Bitriq and others from the People of the Book and the Muslims. Given that it is established that Antioch was the first city to believe, the people of this town, whom Allah mentions as having denied His messengers, were destroyed by a single shout that extinguished them.

Third: The story of Antioch with the disciples (hawariyyun), the companions of the Messiah, came after the revelation of the Torah. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, and more than one of the early scholars mentioned that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, after sending down the Torah, did not destroy any nation entirely with a punishment He sent upon them, but rather commanded the believers after that to fight the polytheists. They cited this in connection with His words: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43]. Accordingly, it is necessary that the people of this town mentioned in the Qur'an were a different town other than Antioch, as more than one of the early scholars also stated; or Antioch, if its name is preserved in this story, is another town other than the well-known and recognized one. This is because this town is not known to have been destroyed, either in the Christian religion or before it. And Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best. End of Ibn Kathir's words.

I say: Among the excellences of the Noble Revelation and its extraordinary eloquence is its brevity in the accounts it relates, and its allusion through them to their spirit and essence, in eagerness for the fruit from the outset, and restriction to the point of benefit, and distance from the method of storytellers and historians. For the purpose of its narratives is reflection and admonition, and there is no need to name those unspecified matters, whatever they may be. Moreover, the exegetes, may Allah have mercy on them, devoted themselves to research, acquisition, and transmission. Those of earlier generations among them saw, in what they saw, that part of knowledge is elaborating the summarized matters of the revelation and clarifying its unspecified matters, until this became a discipline in its own right, and works were composed on it. There is no harm in widening one's knowledge and increasing it by any means whatsoever, especially since the restriction on speaking about the Children of Israel has been lifted. However, one is held accountable if he asserts the specification of some unspecified matter without the basis of decisive evidence (qata'i), for decisive evidence is what is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) or whose chain of transmission is sound up to the infallible one (al-ma'sum), with a soundness free of any flaw. This is lacking in most cases, and our discussion above is one of them. The determination that the town was Antioch and the naming of the messengers were only reported as mawquf (stopping at a companion or follower) and munqati' (with a broken chain), and some of its chain contains accused narrators. For this reason, one who asserts this with certainty may face what has no escape. The best state of the exegete is to proceed with the revelation: in summary regarding what it summarized, and in detail regarding what it detailed. He should take from clarifying its unspecified matters only what is supported by decisive evidence or what sound knowledge does not reject. Otherwise, let him turn away from blackening the pages of books with this, or rather from distorting them.

What led the early scholars to narrate what we are discussing is first their receiving it from figures like Ka'b and Wahb, and the agreement of those of their generation with them on it.

Second, the fame of the town of Antioch in that era, especially since one of the apostles (rusul) of Jesus, peace be upon him, established a place of worship there.

Third, what happened in Antioch when the King of the Romans came, threatening to kill everyone who refused to worship idols. Among the leading ones who refused was a man of standing among the believers. The king wanted him to commit polytheism, but he refused and openly proclaimed monotheism. So he sent him from Antioch in chains and ordered that he be fed to the wild beasts. He was thrown in Rome to two large lions, which swallowed him. When they were presented to them, he rejoiced and exulted at attaining martyrdom in the way of Allah.

Likewise, it is related of a believing man who used to defend the believers in the era of the Romans, out of his zeal and righteousness, that the ruler asked him to renounce his faith. He refused and openly declared the obligation of worshipping the One God and rejecting the worship of what neither harms nor benefits. The ruler threatened to strike him from head to foot. He replied that he rejoiced in the blessing of Allah and His eternal honor. Then the ruler ordered him executed, and he was killed along with his companions. The evidences in this regard are countless and known to whoever gives some attention to what has been written in the histories of the beginnings of the emergence of religions and what their adherents encountered from their enemies and opponents. Thus this noble story has countless confirmations.

Fourth, the fame of the messengers as the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him. They had spread throughout the lands to erase idolatry and to restrain from the major sins and evils that the Roman state was upon at that time.

This, and what Ibn Kathir mentioned about the punishment of annihilation occurring after the revelation of the Torah, requires decisive evidence. Otherwise, many sinful lands were ruined after it, and were destroyed by Allah's empowering whomever He willed over them. The "shout" (sayha) is more general than being a heavenly shout or an earthly shout; it is the shout of whoever was empowered over them for vengeance upon them, until he annihilated their kingdom, subdued their dominion, and erased their authority from existence, even though the punishment of the shout is apparently the first meaning.

In sum, it is sufficient for us from this account to take admonition from it and to understand it in summary. As for specifying it to a particular time or a particular group, that is what gives rise to what arises from it, and we have no need for more than admonition and for leaving aside what has no decisive evidence.

**The second:** Al-Razi mentioned, regarding His words: ﴿When We sent﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14], a subtle point, if it is correct that the messengers mentioned are the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him: that His sending them is like Allah's sending, since it was by His permission and command. And with this the consolation of the Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, is completed, since they come to have the status of messengers.

Then he said: This supports a legal (fiqhi) issue: that the agent of the agent acts by the permission of the principal, and he is the agent of the principal, not the agent of the agent. Therefore he is not dismissed by the dismissal of the agent, but he is dismissed if the first principal dismisses him. End.

**The third:** Regarding His words: ﴿And from the farthest part of the city came a man running﴾ [Ya-Sin: 20], it is an insight for the believers and guidance for them, so that they may be among those who exert their utmost effort in giving sincere counsel, as he did.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 30:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but that they mock him.﴾

﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but that they mock him.﴾ That is: O regret upon them that will occur on the Day of Resurrection, because of their mocking and ridiculing, in the world, of those who gave them sincere counsel, until the matter led them to kill them, as the people of the town did. Or the meaning is the severity of their loss, to the extent that they deserve for both jinn and mankind to feel regret over them. Or the regret is from Him, exalted is He, metaphorically. Its explanation is that regret is what afflicts the one who regrets (p-5003) of remorse, until he remains exhausted, and this is not fitting for Him, exalted is He, so it is made a metaphor, by likening the state of the servants to the state of one over whom God hypothetically feels regret, so He says: "Alas for My servants!" It has been said: this is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, you wonder, and they mock﴾ [al-Saffat: 12] according to the reading with a dammah on the ta', so the calling out to regret is an expression of wonder from Him. The purpose is to magnify their offence, that is, to regard it as a great matter, with wonder from Him. Related by al-Shihab.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[31] ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We have destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾

﴿Have they not seen﴾, i.e., have they not been informed: ﴿how many generations We have destroyed before them﴾, i.e., of the bygone nations; ﴿that they do not return to them﴾, i.e., how they had no return or coming back to this world.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿And indeed, all of them, they will all be brought before Us, present.﴾

﴿And indeed, all⁠﴾ means: of these who are scattered. ﴿Lamma jami'un ladayna muhdarun﴾ means: except that all of them will be brought forth before Us for reckoning and recompense. He reported about (kull) using (jami'), though their meaning is one; because (kull) conveys comprehensiveness, so that not one of them escapes. And (jami') conveys collectivity, and it is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Between the two there is a difference, and for this reason (ajma') occurs as an emphasizing follower of (kull), because it is more specific than it and richer in meaning.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verses 33–35:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[33–35] ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life and brought forth from it grain, so from it they eat. And We made therein gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth within it,﴾ [Yasin: 34] ﴿that they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made. Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Yasin: 35].

﴿And a sign for them﴾ means: a great lesson for the people of Makkah. ﴿The dead earth – We have brought it to life﴾ means: with vegetation (p-5004) so as to indicate the resurrection of the dead. ﴿And We brought forth from it grain, so from it they eat.﴾ ﴿And We made therein gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth within it﴾ [Yasin: 34] ﴿that they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made﴾ [Yasin: 35]. That is: and that they may eat of what their hands have made, which is what is made from it, such as juice (ʿasir) and date syrup (dibs) and the like, as the judge (al-Qadi) preferred.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, their hands made it by planting, irrigating, and digging wells. It was said that this interpretation goes against the apparent meaning, that is, because it requires a figurative usage (tajawwuz). However, it contains a reminder of the pleasure of the fruit of labour and the delight of the soul after it. And in the hadith: "The best earnings are a sale that is accepted and a man's work with his own hand," narrated by Imam Ahmad from Abu Burda. It is also permitted that ma be negative, and the meaning would be: the fruit is by God's creation, not by their action. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Yasin: 35], that is, to the Creator of these great blessings, by worshipping Him alone; and this is a rebuke for their failure to fulfil the obligation of gratitude.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[36] ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of that which they do not know.﴾

﴿Glory be to Him who created the pairs﴾: i.e., the kinds, all of them. ﴿all of them, of what the earth grows﴾: i.e., of what has been mentioned and of other than it. ﴿and of themselves﴾: meaning the male and the female. ﴿and of that which they do not know﴾: i.e., of the kinds and species existing on land and in the sea. And His words, Exalted is He:

On the interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):

[37] ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ This is an explanation of His power (Exalted is He) in time, following what He explained of it in place; that is, We remove it and uncover it from its place. The term "stripping" (salkh), which is the peeling off and removal of the skin from the animal that is skinned, is borrowed for the removal of light. In this there is an indication that the day comes upon the night, just as the thing skinned is from the skin before being skinned, which is like a covering that comes upon the thing covered. Al-Shihab said: "Because the night precedes in custom, in the Sharia and in meaning." ﴿They are in darkness﴾ means they have entered into darkness; it is said "aẓlamnā" (we entered darkness), just as it is said "a'tamnā" (we entered the time of 'atamah, the late night) and "adjaynā" (we entered the time of dujna, the dark part of night).

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[38] ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it. That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾ meaning: to a fixed, predetermined limit at which its daily or annual course comes to an end. It is likened to the resting place of a traveler when he has completed his journey. So the mustaqarr (resting place) is a noun of place, which it traverses in its constant motion and then returns. The point of comparison is arriving at a specific location. The lam is causal (ta'lil), or it carries the meaning of "to" (ila). It has also been said that its mustaqarr is the point where its course ceases at the destruction of the world. And mustaqarr, when it refers to a time, is a noun of time. ﴿That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ meaning: that course, which contains wisdoms, benefits, and advantages, and whose wondrous system of movement and perfect regularity without disorder, is the decree of the One who prevails by His power over every thing that can be decreed, the One who encompasses in knowledge every thing that can be known.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 39:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[39] ﴿And the moon—We have measured it in stations until it returns like the old, dried curved stalk of a palm cluster.﴾

﴿And the moon—We have measured it in stations﴾ meaning: We made for it stations, descending into one of them each night. ﴿Until it returns like the old, dried curved stalk of a palm cluster﴾ meaning: until, when it reaches the last of its stations, it becomes thin and bent like a curved, dried palm cluster (ʿidhq) when a year has passed over it. The ʿurjūn (curved stalk) is the shumrūkh (the stalk of a palm cluster), which is the cluster that bears the fresh dates, and it is called the ʿidhq, with a kasra on the ʿayn. The qadīm (old) is the ʿatīq (aged), and when it becomes old it grows thin, bends, and turns yellow. Thus it is compared to it in three respects.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 40:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[40] ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outpace the day; and each is traveling in an orbit.﴾ (p-5006) ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ meaning: to meet with it at one time, and to encroach upon its domain so that it obscures its light. ﴿Nor does the night outpace the day﴾ meaning: it precedes it by advancing ahead of its time, so that it enters before the day has passed. Or the intended meaning of "night" and "day" is their two signs; that is, nor does the moon outpace the sun, which would be the reverse of the first case; that is, nor is it fitting for the moon to overtake the sun. The meaning according to this is that neither of them enters upon the other within its domain, so that it obscures its light; rather, they follow one another in accordance with the ordinance of Him, exalted is He. Accordingly, the reason for choosing "outpaces" (sabiq) over "overtakes" (mudrik), as in the preceding clause, is that outpacing is suitable to the swiftness of the moon's movement, since outpacing implies speed, whereas overtaking implies slowness. Likewise, the sun is slow in its motion, completing its orbit in a year, while the moon completes it in a month. Thus the sun, owing to its slowness, is worthy of being described as overtaking, and the moon, owing to its swiftness, is worthy of being described as outpacing.

A subtle point:

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: "It is derived from this verse that the day follows the night, which is the well-known position of the jurists. Its demonstration from the verse is that He made the sun, which is the sign of the day, not overtaking the moon, which is the sign of the night."

The negation of overtaking was stated because it is what could possibly occur, and that requires the moon to be ahead and the sun to be following. For one does not say, "the earlier overtook the later," but rather, "the later overtook the earlier." And the negation is worded in accordance with what is possible. Therefore the night is the one followed and the day the follower. If it is said: does this necessarily imply that the night precedes the day, when the verse has explicitly stated that it is not preceding?

The answer is that this is a common obligation. Its explanation: the possible divisions are three: either the day's following of the night, which is the position of the jurists; or its reverse, which is reported from a group of grammarians; or their coexistence. This third division is negated by consensus. So nothing remains except the day following the night and its reverse. This question applies to both of them together, because whoever says the day precedes the night is bound to hold that the rhetoric requires saying: "nor does the night overtake the day," for the later, when its overtaking is negated, is more eloquent than its predecessor (p-5007). Yet it departs from the requirement of His saying, "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," a departure that does not unite the meaning with the wording, for God negated that it should be overtaking, let alone preceding.

Once this is established, the verified answer is that what is negated is the precedence that entails the day's lagging behind the night and another time elapsing between them. In that case the succession is established, and this is the intent of the verse. As for the precedence of the first of two alternating things over the other, it is not considered. Do you not see the response of Moses in His saying: "They are right behind me" [Ta-Ha: 84], where he brought them near to him as an excuse for His saying: "And what hastened you away from your people?" [Ta-Ha: 83]? It is as though he made light of the matter of this haste by their being right behind him. How much more so if he were ahead while they were at his heels, with no distance between them and him? That, if it occurred, the context of the verse would require that it not be counted as haste or precedence. Accordingly, the claim that the day precedes the night would contradict the opening of the verse in a manner that admits no interpretation, for there is a vast gulf between the non-overtaking that indicates delay and following, and precedence. It would also contradict the rest of the verse, for if the night were following and later, it would be more fitting to describe it as not overtaking, without going so far as to describe it as not preceding. And the statement that the night precedes the day would be explicitly in agreement with the opening of the verse, and would be free of any interpretation that fits the composition of the Qur'an. The establishment of the opposite is closer to the truth than the jugular vein. And God is the One who grants success to the right word and its correctness. End.

﴿And each is traveling in an orbit﴾ meaning: each of those mentioned runs in a vast course, like a swimmer in water. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya' what some astronomers said regarding a verse like this one, so refer back to it.

The discussion concerning His saying, may He be exalted:

[41] ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ That is: We carried their children, whom they send (p-5008) on their trade. Al-Shihab said: Its connection to the preceding words, ﴿in a sphere they swim﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40], is not hidden; and the mention of "the laden" (al-mashhun) is stronger in expressing the favour of their safety therein, or because it is further from danger. It was also said that the intended meaning is the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him. Thus it is singular (mufrad), and its definiteness is for a known reference (al-ahd), and the meaning is the carrying of their earliest forefathers, by whom the survival of the species is preserved, when the flood became general, and they were saved with Nuh in the ark. It is a sign because the survival of their progeny and their deliverance in a single ship is a wondrous work and a great power. Some preferred the first interpretation, because the second requires interpretation (ta'wil). I see the second as deserving preference, by the rule of interpreting things according to their like and counterparts wherever a way exists, since it is closer and more solid. Its counterpart has come in the verse: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the flowing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11] ﴿That We might make it for you a reminder, and that a retaining ear might retain it﴾ [al-Haqqah: 12]. And although the verse ﴿And His are the ships raised high in the sea like landmarks﴾ [al-Rahman: 24] and similar verses occur in the counterpart of the first, the term "carrying" is unified in the two verses, so the two are close to one another.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 42:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And We have created for them of the like of it that they ride.﴾

﴿And We have created for them of the like of it﴾, i.e., of the like of the ship (al-falak), ﴿that they ride﴾, i.e., of the camels, for they are the "ships of the land" (safa'in al-barr) because of how much they carry, to the point that the usage of "ship" (safina) for them became widespread, as it has been said: "Ships of the land, and the mirage is their seas." Or ﴿that they ride﴾, i.e., of the boats and skiffs, according to the second interpretation, which is that by the ship (al-falak) is meant the ship of Noah.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 43:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[43] ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them, nor are they rescued.﴾

﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them﴾ meaning: there is no helper for them, or no one among them seeking help, or no seeking of help. This is because al-ṣarīkh (the one who cries out for help) may be the one who gives aid (al-mughīth), the one who seeks aid (al-mustaghīth), and the one who cries out (al-ṣārikh). It is also a verbal noun of the triliteral form, like al-ṣurākh (crying out), and is used metaphorically for aid (al-ighātha), because the one who gives aid calls out to the one who seeks his aid and cries out for him, saying: "Help and victory have come to you." Al-Mubarrad recited at the beginning of al-Kāmil:

Whenever a frightened crier came to us, the crying out to him was the striking of the necks (of the swift camels) (qarʿ al-ẓanābīb).

That is, when a seeker of aid came to us, our giving aid to him was earnest support of him.

﴿Nor are they rescued﴾ meaning: they are not saved from death by it.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[44] ﴿Except as a mercy from Us, and as enjoyment for a time.﴾

﴿Except as a mercy from Us, and as enjoyment for a time.﴾ That is: rather, We showed them mercy and gave them enjoyment until a term appointed for them, in which they will die after being saved from the death of drowning. From here Abu al-Tayyib (Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi) took his words:

Though I be saved, nothing remains; but I have been spared from one death's hour unto another death's hour.

The Discussion of the Interpretation of His, Exalted is He, Saying:

[45] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you and what is behind you, that perhaps you may receive mercy."﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you"﴾ i.e., of the events that passed among the nations that denied the messengers.

﴿and what is behind you﴾ i.e., of the punishment prepared in the Hereafter, or the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, or the reverse of that, or what of your sins has preceded and what has followed. ﴿That perhaps you may receive mercy﴾ i.e., through your heeding and your thankfulness. The response to (idha, "when") is omitted, indicated by His saying:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[46] ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾

﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord⦄ i.e., those that indicate the truthfulness of the Messengers, ﴿except that they turn away from it⦄ by denying it and averting themselves from believing in it.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[47] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed, if He willed? You are only in manifest error."﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you"﴾ means: give charity to the poor from God's wealth which He has given you. ﴿Those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed, if He willed? You are only in manifest error"﴾ means: in that you command us to do what opposes God's will. Their statement is either mockery or the product of genuine belief. It is permissible that ﴿You are only in manifest error﴾ is God's reply to them, or that it recounts the reply of the believers. In this verse there is a most forceful rebuke against relating what is narrated of misers in their excuses, using the same kind of argument with which the polytheists led themselves astray, and in their echoing it. For that is from baseness, stinginess of soul, and corrupt disposition, even though some people cite it for amusement or for novelty, as al-Jahiz did in his book "al-Bukhala'" (The Misers). May God forgive him.

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[48] ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ They mean the promise of the Resurrection.

(p-5011) Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[49] ﴿They await but a single Blast, which will seize them while they are still disputing.﴾

﴿They await but a single Blast, which will seize them while they are still disputing.﴾ That is: they dispute with one another in their markets and their dealings. That is, it will overtake them while they are in their security and heedless of it. The reading of "yakhissimūn" is with a fatḥah on the yā' and a kasrah on the khā', due to the meeting of two sukūns (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The original form, which is the basis, is "yakhtasimūn": the tā' was made sukūn and assimilated (idghām) into the ṣād, and then the khā' was given a kasrah due to the meeting of two sukūns.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their people.﴾

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾: that is, they will not be able to give any instruction concerning any of their affairs, as a bequest.

﴿Nor will they return to their people﴾: that is, they will not be able to return to their families so as to see their condition; rather, they will die right where the Blast (al-Sayhah) overtakes them.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and behold, they will rush from their graves to their Lord.﴾

﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾, i.e., for the Resurrection. ﴿Behold, they will rush from their graves﴾, i.e., from the graves. ﴿To their Lord they will rush﴾, i.e., they will run hastily, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves swiftly﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. [ 58 ] On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful.﴾

That is: for them there is peace, said to them as a word proceeding from Him, exalted is He. So "salam" (peace) may be the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted; or it is a substitute (badal) for "ma" (what); or it is a predicate whose omitted subject is "ma" (what, i.e., "it is peace"); or it is a subject whose predicate is the verb governing "qawlan" (a word), meaning: peace that is said to them as a word; or it is a subject whose predicate is "min Rabbin" (from a Lord), and "qawlan" is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for the content of the sentence, which, together with its governing verb, is parenthetical between the subject and the predicate. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, greets them with peace, honouring them, as in His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be, "Peace."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 60:

(p-5014) The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[60] ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ This is a rebuke from Him, Exalted is He, to the disbelievers, said to them as a means of establishing the proof against them (ilzam lil-hujjah). His, Exalted is He, charge (ahd) to them is the covenant of primordial nature (fitrah), as stated by al-Qashani. Or it is what He established for them of rational proofs (hujaj 'aqliyyah) and revealed proofs (hujaj sam'iyyah), which command the worship of Him alone and the rejection of the worship of others.

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾

﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ That is: and that you single Me out for worship, for it is the right (sawi) way. In the indefiniteness of the word (path) there is an indication that it is a path that is eloquent in its straightness, comprehensive of everything that it must be upon, and the root of a rank which description falls short of reaching; so the tanwin is for magnification.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[62] ﴿And he had certainly led astray from among you a great multitude. Then did you not use reason?﴾

﴿And he had certainly led astray﴾, i.e., Satan, and misguided [them] into associating partners with God. ﴿From among you a great multitude﴾, i.e., a great number of creatures before you. So the terrible punishment befell them. ﴿Then did you not use reason?﴾, i.e., were you not among the people of intellect? It is a rebuke for you to be among them, when the proofs and warnings had been established.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[65] ﴿This Day We shall seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾

﴿This Day We shall seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ That is: when they deny what they committed in this world and swear that they did not do it, then God seals their mouths and makes their limbs speak. Al-Razi said: Regarding the sealing of the mouths there are several interpretations, the strongest of which is that God silences their tongues so that they cannot speak with them, and makes their limbs speak so that they bear witness against them. This is easy for God's power. As for silencing, there is no doubt about it. As for making them speak, that is because the tongue is a member that moves by a specific motion, so just as it is possible for it to move by that motion, it is possible for other members to move by a similar motion, and God is capable of all possible things.

The other interpretation is that they will not speak at all, because their excuses will be cut off and their veils torn away. They will stand with bowed heads, in the standing of the despairing one who has lost hope, finding no excuse to offer and no room for repentance to seek forgiveness. The speech of the hands is the manifestation of matters to such a degree that denial is no longer possible, until the hands and the eyes speak of it. As the saying goes: "The walls weep for the owner of the house," indicating the manifestation of sorrow. The first interpretation is the correct one. End of quotation.

That is: it is possible and not impossible, so the reality is not out of reach. This is supported by the verse: ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you bear witness against us?" They will say, "God has made us speak, who made everything speak."﴾ [Fussilat: 21]

(p. 5016) Among the elegant pieces of some literati of the age is what he composed about the phonograph (al-funughraf), citing it as evidence for this, and he said:

By the speech of the phonograph there is for us a proof of the speech of the limbs and of inanimate things.

In it is an example, for every one who reflects, of the beginning of creation and of the Return.

A single one manages its affairs with forms, by which sounds flow like ink.

A pen records its figures on a tablet, according to what is willed and intended.

After its completion it passes like lightning, and no trace of it appears in the cosmos.

You think it has gone away as foam, just as the people of ʿĀd went away by a wind.

And its sweet echo remains in it, like spirits stripped of matter.

Whenever the Manager wills for it a return, and its appearance is desired in every assembly,

He sets the trumpets in motion with instruments by force, so its dead is raised after sleep.

This is an instrument made by a servant; how then with the making of the Creator of servants?

Blessed is He who restores all creation at once by the blast of His trumpet on the Day of Calling.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[66] ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path, but how could they see?﴾

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path, but how could they see?﴾ That is: if Allah, Exalted is He, willed, He would have wiped out their eyes. So if they attempted to race to the road that was traveled by them, they would not be able to, because of their blindness.

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[67] ﴿And if We willed, We could have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed, nor would they return.﴾

﴿And if We willed, We could have transformed them﴾, i.e., by altering their forms and nullifying their faculties; ﴿in their places﴾, i.e., in their locations; ﴿so they would not be able to proceed﴾, i.e., to go forward; ﴿nor would they return﴾, i.e., nor return (back). That is, they would not be able to leave their places. He placed the verb in its position for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). And if it means "they would not return from their disbelief," then it is conjoined to the clause "they would not be able." The intent is that, through their disbelief and their breaking of the covenant that was made with them, they deserve to have this done to them. But We did not do it, out of the all-encompassing mercy and in keeping with the wisdom of granting them respite.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[68] ﴿And whomever We give long life, We reverse him in creation; will they not then reason?﴾

﴿And whomever We give long life﴾, i.e., We prolong his lifespan. ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾, i.e., through the diminishing of his powers and the weakness of his frame, until he returns to a state resembling that of the child in the weakness of his body, the scantness of his reason, and his emptiness of knowledge, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5]. ﴿Will they not then reason?﴾, i.e., whoever is able to do this is able to obliterate and transform, and to do whatever He wills.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[69] ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an.﴾

﴿We did not teach him poetry﴾ means: so that he would produce poetry. This is a refutation of their claim that he, may the blessings of God be upon him, is a poet who brought poetry. They compared him to one who is skilled in poetry through reading the collections and memorizing much of them. But how could what was revealed to him resemble poetry, when it is not poetry either in wording, because it lacks its metre and rhyme, or in meaning, because poetry is imaginings, whereas this is judgments, creeds, laws, and realities?

﴿Nor is it fitting for him﴾ means: nor is it proper for his station, because the abode of prophethood and messengership is far above poetry and its composition, since poets often utter falsehood, exaggeration, and departure from the paths of truth. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is only﴾, that is, the Qur'an which he recites, ﴿a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition and guidance from Him, exalted is He; ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾, that is, a heavenly book whose matter and realities are clear. So there is no connection whatsoever between it and poetry (p-٥٠١٨).

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 70:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿That he may warn whoever is alive, and that the Word may take effect against the disbelievers.﴾

﴿That he may warn whoever is alive﴾ means: whoever is rational and reflective, for the heedless is like the dead. ﴿And that the Word may take effect﴾ means: and the word of punishment becomes due. ﴿Against the disbelievers﴾ means: those who turn away from following him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 71:

﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made﴾ i.e., of that which We Ourselves undertook to create, and none other than Us can bring it into being. ﴿cattle, and they are their owners﴾ i.e., they dispose of them with the disposal of owners (al-mulak), or they are masters and subduers of them, as the poet said:

"I have become one who does not bear the weapon, nor do I hold the halter of the camel if it bolts."

[72] ﴿And We have subjugated them to them, so some of them are their mounts, and of them they eat.﴾

﴿And We have subjugated them to them﴾ means: We made them docile, not wild (wahshiyyah).

﴿So some of them are their mounts﴾ means: their means of riding (markub).

﴿And of them they eat﴾ means: they benefit by eating their flesh.

[73] ﴿And for them therein are benefits and drinks. Will they not then be grateful?﴾

﴿And for them therein are benefits﴾ — i.e., from their hides, wool, and fur. ﴿And drinks﴾ — i.e., from their milk. ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ — i.e., that they would worship the Bestower of these magnificent blessings in their various kinds.

[74] ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be helped﴾.

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be helped﴾: i.e., that they (the gods) would help them against the calamities that befall them.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 36, verse 75:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[75] ﴿They are unable to help them, though they are a host brought forward for them.﴾

﴿They are unable to help them, though they are a host brought forward for them﴾: that is, for their gods, ﴿a host brought forward﴾, meaning prepared for their service and for defending them. So how could they help them, while they are in such a state of helplessness and weakness? That is, rather, the matter is the reverse. It has also been said: the meaning is "brought forward behind them into the Fire," and making them "a host" on this reading is mockery and derision. Likewise the lam in ﴿for them﴾ denotes benefit.

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[76] ﴿So let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they declare.﴾

﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾, i.e., concerning Allah, the Exalted, with atheism and polytheism; or concerning you, with denial and harm. ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they declare﴾, i.e., We will recompense them for it. He expressed their recompense by His knowledge, the Exalted, because it necessarily entails it; for the knowledge of the powerful King regarding what His enemy, the disbeliever, has done necessitates His recompense and retribution. The mention of what is concealed (sirr) first serves to show that the knowledge of the Exalted encompasses all things, such that the concealed and the open are equal in His sight. Or it points to the importance of reforming the inner state, for that is the foundation of the matter.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[77] ﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary?﴾

﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ That is: a disputer with falsehood (p-5020), clear in contention. This is a second consolation, by belittling what they say in comparison with their denial of the Resurrection (al-hashr). The first, which is His saying �były: ﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾ [Ya-Sin: 76] and what follows, was ordered for the sake of His concern for his status, may the blessings of Allah be upon him.

Al-Tibi said: This is conjoined with ﴿Do they not see﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71] before it, and the common factor between each of them is that they are built on inversion (al-ta'kis): He created for him what He created so that he would give thanks, but he disbelieved and denied the blessings and the Benefactor; and He created him from a filthy drop so that he would be submissive and humble, but he transgressed, became arrogant, and disputed.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[78] ﴿And he presents to Us a parable and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾

﴿And he presents to Us a parable﴾ meaning: in declaring resurrection far-fetched and denying it. ﴿And forgets his own creation﴾ meaning: that We created him. ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ meaning: crumbling, most thoroughly worn away, utterly far from life. The word is not feminine because it is a noun for what has decayed of the bones, solid and not a descriptive adjective, like "rummah" (bone-remnant) and "rufat" (crumbled fragments). Or it is a form on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), but since its usage became predominant for something not described, it was assigned to the nouns and so was not made feminine. Or it is in the sense of maf'ul (passive) from "rammahu," meaning "abla-hu" (he wore it out). Its original root is eating, from "rammat al-ibil al-hashish" (the camels ate the grass). It is as if the earth has eaten what has decayed. Al-Azhari said: since "izaman" (bones), being on the pattern of the singular, like "kitab" and "qirab," ramim was treated according to its treatment, and he cited evidence for this. Al-Shihab said: and this is strange.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[79] ﴿Say: He will give them life who brought them into being the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation.﴾

﴿Say: He will give them life who brought them into being the first time⦆ That is: the power of the Creator is not measured by the power of created beings. Rather, His re-creation is measured only against His original origination. ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation⦆ That is: it is not impossible for Him to gather the parts after they have been scattered, given His knowledge of their origins, their details, their places, and the way of joining them to one another.

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted:**

[80] ﴿He who has made for you fire from the green tree, and behold, you kindle from it.﴾

﴿He who has made for you fire from the green tree, and behold, you kindle from it.﴾ That is: He who created this tree from water until it became green and fresh, so it bore fruit and ripened, then returned it until it became dry firewood with which fire is kindled. Thus He is the One who does what He wills, able to do what He intends, and nothing can prevent Him.

Qatada said: The One who brought fire out of this tree is able to resurrect it (the dead). It was also said: what is meant is the tree of al-Markh and al-Affar (from the trees of the desert) in the land of the Hijaz. A man who wanted to strike fire, and had no flint with him, would take from it two green sticks and strike one against the other, and fire would be produced between them just as from flint.

This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Al-Affar is the upper flint-stick (al-zand), and al-Markh is the lower tinder-stick (al-zandah), in the position of the male and the female. Al-Jawhari reversed this, making al-Markh the male and al-Affar the female, and the wording supports him; however, the first view is supported by the words of the poet:

*When al-Markh does not kindle beneath al-Affar, and withholds its spark, it is not made to produce fire.*

Abu Ziyad said: Among all trees, none kindles fire more readily than al-Markh. Sometimes al-Markh grows dense and intertwined, the wind blows, its branches rub against one another, and they kindle and burn the valley, and we have not seen this with the rest of the trees. Al-Azhari said: The Arabs use al-Markh and al-Affar as an example of lofty nobility. They say: "Every tree has fire, but al-Markh and al-Affar have excelled (istamjada)." That is, their fire is more abundant than in the rest of the trees. And (istamjada) means: became abundant and surpassed. This is because these two trees are among the trees with the most fire, and their tinder is the swiftest to kindle. There is also a proverb: "Strike with al-Affar or al-Markh, then tighten if you wish, or loosen." It is also said: "Every tree has fire except al-Unnab (the jujube)."

(p-٥٠٢٢) Al-Shihab said: For this reason a pestle for fullers is made from it. Then he recited a verse of his own:

*O jujube tree, your fire has kindled in my heart, and the jujube is not of the trees of fire.*

End of quotation.

The purpose is that it is not impossible for Him, the Exalted, to restore the temperament (mizaj, the balance of qualities in a body) to which the soul was attached after its complete annihilation. For He who transforms the temperament of a moist tree into the temperament of fire, which is hot and dry in actuality, despite the watery nature of the tree that opposes it, is more capable of restoring freshness to what was once fresh, after dryness and decay have befallen it.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[81] ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, indeed; and He is the Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., despite their great bulk, ﴿able to create the likes of them﴾, i.e., in smallness and weakness, a second time, after having created them the first time? ﴿Yes﴾, i.e., He is the One who is able. ﴿And He is the Creator﴾, i.e., the one who creates abundantly, time after time. ﴿The All-Knowing﴾, i.e., the one whose knowledge of things is vast.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[82] ﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

﴿Indeed, His command﴾ means: His exalted affair, or His penetrating word. ﴿When He intends a thing﴾ means: when His will becomes attached to bringing a thing into existence. ﴿That He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ means: so it comes into being at His command.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿So exalted is He in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

﴿So exalted is He in whose hand is the dominion of all things⦆ is a declaration of His transcendence above what the polytheists attribute to Him, and an expression of wonder that they should say about Him what they have said. He is the Owner of everything and the One who disposes of it without any restraint or any rival contending with Him. ﴿And to Him you will be returned⦆ means: after death, so that He will recompense you for your deeds.

Benefit:

Ibn Kathir said: "Al-mulk (dominion) and al-malakut (sovereignty) are one in meaning, like rahmah and rahamut, rahbah and rahabut, and jabr and jabarut. Some people claim that al-mulk is the world of bodies and al-malakut is the world of spirits. The correct view is the first, which is the view held by the majority of the exegetes and others." End of quotation.

Some scholars have said: al-malakut is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah) derived from al-mulk, so it means complete dominion. And Allah is the All-Knowing, the All-Knowing of all things.
